topics.topic: Accepted JSON number spellings, canonicalization, and resulting runtime numeric semantics
questions: What exact parsing and acceptance algorithm applies to every JSON number, especially internally produced Python `int` values that have no submitted spelling, and does decoding accepted canonical bytes preserve an integer as its mathematical integer or treat all numbers with RFC 8785 binary64 semantics?
Exactly which finite JSON number spellings are accepted or refused, including plain integers, decimal fractions and exponent forms that round when converted to IEEE-754 binary64?

After canonicalization changes the decimal spelling of an accepted exactly representable large integer, which integer does a function, schema validator, equality comparison, and stored value observe: the submitted mathematical integer or the integer obtained by parsing the canonical digits as a Python `int`?

What numeric value and Python type must be stored and delivered after canonicalisation: the mathematical integer originally submitted, the IEEE-754 value represented by the canonical text, or the integer obtained by parsing the canonical decimal text with Python’s arbitrary-precision parser?

judgement.why: P1 judged the same question about accepted JSON number spellings, canonicalization, and Python runtime numeric values on the same texts.

precedent.topic: Exact admission predicate for JSON and Python numeric values
quotes: canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.

canonical_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise NonCanonicalValueError, with a reason naming the first offending item in text order, when json_text is not one well-formed JSON value, when an object repeats a member name at any depth, when it holds a non-finite number (NaN, Infinity or -Infinity tokens, which the default Python parser would accept and therefore MUST be rejected explicitly), when a number written without a fraction or exponent lies outside plus or minus (2 to the power 53 minus 1) and is neither held exactly by an IEEE double nor written exactly as that double's ECMAScript shortest round-trip form — 100000000000000000000, which a double holds exactly, and 18014398509481990, the form JCS writes for 1.801439850948199e+16, are each that double, so canonical bytes always parse again to the same bytes —, when the value nests deeper than the imported RELEASE_CEILING_JSON_DEPTH_MAX constant, the depth of a scalar being 0 and of an array or object one more than its deepest member, 1 when it has none, found while parsing and never by a recursion deeper than that constant, or when a string holds a lone surrogate.

runner_source: [BEHAVIOR] When run returned, the program MUST write one returned message: whether the value is a dict with only str keys and, for each key, its form — json for a value port whose value json.dumps accepts with sort_keys=True, separators (',', ':'), ensure_ascii=False and allow_nan=False (for a many value port, a list), file for a file port whose value is bytes, file_list for a many file port whose value is a list of bytes, not_representable otherwise and for a key that is no output port.
precedent.why: State 8 specifies the complete spelling-sensitive JSON predicate and the serialization path by which Python numeric outputs acquire JSON spelling before canonicalization.

topics.topic: Depth measurement scope and root for surface requests
questions: Is depth measured on the complete MCP request, independently on each submitted value/schema/constant, or both, and are request-envelope levels counted against a run input's limit?

Is depth measured from the request envelope, independently from each submitted domain value/schema, or both; and how can an input of depth exactly 64 be accepted inside a request if the envelope also has maximum depth 64?
Is the depth limit applied to the complete request envelope, to the operation arguments object, or separately only to submitted domain values such as each run input, constant and schema?

judgement.why: P2 judged the same question about the roots and scopes used to measure request and embedded-value depth on the same texts.

precedent.topic: Root and scope used to measure JSON depth
quotes: answer_request: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Before any other bound is checked and before the arguments are walked or canonicalised, the depth of the arguments MUST be within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_JSON_DEPTH_MAX constant — a scalar 0, an array or object one more than its deepest member, 1 when it has none —, measured without recursion, else invalid_request; a deeper request never reaches a recursive walk.

A value in a request is JSON text in a string field and a file is base64 text, so that `surface` sees the exact text it canonicalizes, duplicate member names included; an answer carries values as JSON text and file bytes as base64.

canonical_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise NonCanonicalValueError, with a reason naming the first offending item in text order, when json_text is not one well-formed JSON value, when an object repeats a member name at any depth, when it holds a non-finite number (NaN, Infinity or -Infinity tokens, which the default Python parser would accept and therefore MUST be rejected explicitly), when a number written without a fraction or exponent lies outside plus or minus (2 to the power 53 minus 1) and is neither held exactly by an IEEE double nor written exactly as that double's ECMAScript shortest round-trip form — 100000000000000000000, which a double holds exactly, and 18014398509481990, the form JCS writes for 1.801439850948199e+16, are each that double, so canonical bytes always parse again to the same bytes —, when the value nests deeper than the imported RELEASE_CEILING_JSON_DEPTH_MAX constant, the depth of a scalar being 0 and of an array or object one more than its deepest member, 1 when it has none, found while parsing and never by a recursion deeper than that constant, or when a string holds a lone surrogate.
precedent.why: The later contracts measure the tools/call arguments object and separately canonicalize and depth-check each JSON text carried inside it.

topics.topic: Depth-check ordering and refusal precedence for invalid surface requests
questions: For a request that is over-depth and also has an unknown token, unknown operation, malformed schema or another failing field, which refusal wins, and at what point in A16's request order is the depth check applied?
For a request that is too deep and also has an unknown token, malformed schema, or another request-level fault, which refusal wins and at what exact point is depth checked?

judgement.why: P3 judged the same question about depth-check placement and refusal precedence for invalid surface requests on the same texts.

precedent.topic: Validation and refusal precedence for over-depth requests
quotes: answer_request: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST check one request in exactly this order, the first failure deciding: the byte length of request_bytes is within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant, else invalid_request; authenticate_token with presented_token gives an Actor, else unauthorized with one fixed reason that reveals nothing about any record; for tools/call, the message names a catalogue operation and fits that operation's request model with no unknown field — a field typed X | None fitting when it is absent or JSON null; the fit is pydantic's in JSON mode, the request model's model_validate_json over the canonical JSON text of the arguments with strict=True, since strict validation of Python objects refuses an enum given as its value string and a tuple given as a JSON array, which is how every request carries them; a ValueError the fit raises (pydantic's ValidationError is one) is raised again as InvalidRequestError, so translate_failure answers invalid_request, never internal_error — and every bound below, else invalid_request; the actor may call that operation by the actor table, else not_permitted; only then is the operation's handler called (A16 rule 1).

answer_request: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Before any other bound is checked and before the arguments are walked or canonicalised, the depth of the arguments MUST be within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_JSON_DEPTH_MAX constant — a scalar 0, an array or object one more than its deepest member, 1 when it has none —, measured without recursion, else invalid_request; a deeper request never reaches a recursive walk.

answer_request: [FIELD_ASSIGNMENT] Before any handler runs, MUST replace every JSON text the request carries — the json_text of each RequestJsonValue and RequestConstant, the value_schema of every Port and RequestConstant, the guard_value of every EdgeGuard — by its canonical form obtained from canonical_bytes; a NonCanonicalValueError there is invalid_request, so modules below receive only canonical JSON (A01 rule 1).

answer_request: [VALIDATION_ERROR] A refusal decided before the operation is known is a JSON-RPC error response whose error is {code, message: the refusal code, data: the RefusalAnswer as {code, reason}}: a body over the size ceiling is -32600 invalid_request; a token refusal -32600 unauthorized; a body that is not JSON -32700 invalid_request; a body that is not one JSON object — a batch array included — or whose jsonrpc is not "2.0" -32600 invalid_request; a request whose method is none of initialize, ping, tools/list and tools/call -32601 invalid_request; a tools/call whose params is not an object with a string name and an object arguments, or whose name is no catalogue operation, -32602 invalid_request.
precedent.why: State 8 fixes size and authentication before argument depth, depth before other argument bounds and canonicalization, and separately fixes malformed-envelope handling.
